fullDescription:
The three stops that make a first visit to Ha Long complete, in one day from Hanoi.

Sung Sot, the Surprise Cave, is the biggest in the bay. A climb from the jetty opens into two enormous lit chambers, and the second is large enough that the scale only registers once you are standing in it. French explorers found it in the 1900s and named it the Grotte des Surprises, which is still the name locals translate back.

Luon Cave is its opposite. A low tunnel runs through the base of a karst into a lagoon enclosed by cliffs, and you pass through by bamboo boat or kayak because at high tide the ceiling is barely above your head. Inside, the walls cut the wind and the water goes completely still.

Ti Top Island gives you the photograph. Around 400 steps climb to a viewpoint where the karsts run to the horizon in every direction, and there is a beach at the bottom for afterwards. The island is named for a Soviet cosmonaut who visited with Ho Chi Minh in 1962.

The bus uses the expressway, which keeps Hanoi to Ha Long at around two and a half hours each way rather than four on the old road. An English-speaking guide is with you for the whole trip.

This is the complete first-visit day: the big cave, the hidden lagoon and the view, with nothing left you would regret missing.

We book with Vietnam Vacations Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers the English-speaking guide and round-trip highway bus transfer with Hanoi pickup and drop-off.

Six hours on the bay. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Sung Sot: two vast lit chambers, the bay's largest cave
Luon Cave by bamboo boat, under a head-high ceiling
Ti Top: 400 steps to karsts running to the horizon
Named for a Soviet cosmonaut who came with Ho Chi Minh
Highway route keeps the transfer to two and a half hours

fullDescription:
A premium day cruise with a jacuzzi on deck, departing from Ninh Binh rather than Hanoi.

The Ninh Binh pickup is what makes this worth finding. Almost every Ha Long day cruise runs out of Hanoi, which leaves anyone already in Ninh Binh with a three-hour backtrack to the capital just to come back out again. This one collects you where you are.

That matters because Ninh Binh and Ha Long are the classic northern pairing: the same limestone karst rising out of rice paddies in one and out of the sea in the other. Doing them back to back without returning to Hanoi in between saves most of a day.

The jacuzzi is on the sun deck, which on a cruise through the karsts is a better place to be than the dining room. A buffet is served on board.

Drop-off point is your choice of options, so you can end the day in Ha Long, go back to Ninh Binh, or continue to Hanoi depending on where your trip goes next. Confirm which one you want at booking.

The bay itself is roughly 1,600 limestone islands, the tops of a karst range that stayed above water as sea levels rose after the last ice age.

fullDescription:
A performance staged inside a limestone cave, with a banquet, built to fit a cruise ship's port call.

Dragon Pearl Cave is a natural cavern fitted out as a theatre. The show draws on the legend that gives the bay its name: a mother dragon sent down to defend Vietnam from invaders, spitting jade and pearl that hardened into the islands still standing in the water outside. Ha Long means descending dragon, and this is where that story is told.

What makes it work is the room. Limestone caverns have acoustics that no built theatre reproduces, and the rock is lit rather than hidden, so the cave is part of the staging instead of a venue.

A banquet follows, served either as lunch or dinner depending on your sailing.

Four and a half hours with round-trip transfer between the cave and Halong International Port is built around a ship's schedule. If you are on a cruise call and want something that is not another boat, this is the counter-programme: you have already seen the bay from the water, and this is the same bay's story from inside the rock it is made of.

It also runs in weather that stops the small boats, since the entire programme is under cover.

We book with Up Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers the entertainment programme in Dragon Pearl Cave, dinner or lunch, and round-trip transfer between the cave and Halong International Port.

Four and a half hours. Minimum one day's notice.

The descending-dragon legend that names the bay
Cave acoustics and lit rock as part of the staging
Banquet served as lunch or dinner to suit your sailing

fullDescription:
A full day in Lan Ha Bay, which is the quiet half of this coastline and the harder one to reach.

Lan Ha lies south of Ha Long proper, off Cat Ba Island: around 300 islands of the same drowned karst, with a fraction of the boats because the big fleet concentrates north. The scenery is identical. The traffic is not.

A full day rather than a six-hour cruise is what lets the activities be real. Kayaking here goes into water the cruise boats cannot follow you into, and swimming happens off the boat in sheltered bays rather than at a fixed beach stop with two hundred other people.

The bay is also where Cat Ba's floating fishing villages are. Families live on rafts with grouper and snapper pens beneath them, and the boats work around them rather than past them.

There are two ways to join. From Hanoi you take the shuttle bus from the Old Quarter, which makes it a long day with the expressway at both ends. From Cat Ba it is a short car transfer, which is the better version if you are already staying on the island.

Check which option yours is when booking, because the difference is about five hours.

We book with Anh Tourist Hanoi Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers shuttle bus pickup and drop-off in the Hanoi Old Quarter on the Hanoi option, or round-trip car transfers on the Cat Ba option.

Full day. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Lan Ha: the same karst as Ha Long, a fraction of the boats
A full day, so kayaking and swimming are real rather than stops
Kayak into water the cruise boats cannot follow

fullDescription:
A private full-day shore excursion covering the city behind the bay, for passengers who have already seen the water.

Most cruise calls at Ha Long put everyone back on a boat. This goes the other way, into the working city of a few hundred thousand people that the pier belongs to, which almost no visitor ever sees.

Quang Ninh Museum is the reason to do it. It is a black glass box on the waterfront by the Spanish architect Salvador Perez Arroyo, and the facade mirrors the bay so completely that the building half disappears into it. Inside it runs from the region's marine geology through the coal-mining history that actually built this city, including a reconstructed mine shaft.

Long Tien Pagoda sits beneath Bai Tho Mountain and is the largest in the city, built in the 1940s in the style of Hanoi's older temples.

The markets are where Ha Long eats, at local prices rather than pier prices, and the Dragon Pearl Cave show closes the day: a performance staged inside a natural limestone cavern, telling the descending-dragon legend that gives the bay its name.

Private transfer from Halong International Port throughout means the timing bends to your ship rather than a group schedule, which on a port call is worth more than it sounds.

Entrance fees to all sites and an English-speaking guide are included.

We book with Up Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers round-trip private transfer from Halong International Port, the guide and all entrance fees.

Eight hours. Minimum one day's notice.

Quang Ninh Museum: a glass box that mirrors the bay

fullDescription:
Northern Vietnam's two headline landscapes across two days, run as one booking out of Hanoi.

Ninh Binh and Ha Long are the same limestone in two settings. In Ninh Binh the karst towers rise out of rice paddies with a river running between them, which is why it gets called the inland bay; in Ha Long they rise out of the sea. Doing them on consecutive days is what makes the pair land as one landscape rather than two separate attractions.

Booking them together rather than separately solves the logistics. Both run out of Hanoi, both are two to three hours away in different directions, and arranging them as two independent day trips means two early starts, two sets of transfers and a day in between with nothing in it.

Hotel pickup and drop-off is in the Hanoi Old Quarter at both ends, and an English-speaking guide stays with you across both days rather than handing you between operators.

Transport runs by limousine or bus depending on the option chosen. Over two days and several hundred kilometres that is the main difference between the price points, so check which one yours is.

Two days is the minimum that gives each place a real visit. A single day trying to cover both is mostly road.
